children.note: The first three years of primary school, after pre-primary. Children build strong reading, writing and counting, and learn by doing, playing and exploring the world around them.

nodeData.note: The first three years of primary school, after pre-primary. Children build strong reading, writing and counting, and learn by doing, playing and exploring the world around them.

children.note: The stage that follows PP1 and PP2.
Lower primary is three years: Grade 1, Grade 2 and Grade 3.

manas.q: Which grades make up lower primary?

children.note: The 2019 curriculum framework says children enter Grade 1 at about six years old. Check your school's admission rules.

manas.q: At about what age do children start Grade 1?

children.note: Children arrive from two years of pre-primary, where they learnt through play. Grade 1 builds gently on that.

manas.q: What comes just before Grade 1?

children.note: Pre-primary and lower primary together make up Early Years Education in the CBC structure.

manas.q: Which two levels make up Early Years Education?

children.note: Children learn through activities, songs, games, stories and real objects, not only by copying from the board.
KICD's Grade 1–3 page lists nine learning areas. Names below are the official ones.
Children listen, speak, read and write in English: sounds, words, short stories, and simple sentences about daily life.

manas.q: What is the English learning area called in Grades 1–3?

children.note: Watoto husikiliza, huzungumza, husoma na kuandika kwa Kiswahili: hadithi, nyimbo na sentensi fupi.
Counting, numbers, adding and taking away, shapes, measuring and money. Course books call it Mathematical Activities.

manas.q: Which learning area covers counting, shapes and money?

children.note: Exploring home, school and nature: weather, plants, animals, water, keeping clean and staying safe.

manas.q: Which learning area explores weather, plants and water?

children.note: Drawing, colouring, modelling, music, singing, dance and movement games that grow imagination and healthy bodies.

manas.q: Which learning area covers art, music and movement?

children.note: Learning in the language of the local community, through stories, songs and talk, to value home language and culture.

manas.q: Which learning area uses the local community language?

children.note: Christian Religious Education: Bible stories, prayer, and values like love, kindness and sharing.

manas.q: What does CRE stand for?

children.note: Islamic Religious Education: stories, short surahs, prayer and good manners taught in Islam.

manas.q: What does IRE stand for?

children.note: Hindu Religious Education: stories, festivals, prayer and values from the Hindu faith.
Strong reading and writing in two languages is a big goal of these years.
Children learn letter sounds, blend them into words, and read short words aloud.
They read simple stories and answer questions about what happened and why.
From tracing letters to writing their name, then short sentences about home and friends.
Show-and-tell, news time and retelling stories help children speak clearly.
English and Kiswahili are both learnt, so children can read and talk in both.
Maths starts with real things children can touch and count.
Counting objects, reading and writing numbers, and putting them in order.
Simple sums using bottle tops, beans or sticks before written work.
Spotting circles, squares and triangles around the home, and making patterns.
Comparing long and short, heavy and light, full and empty, using everyday items.
Recognising Kenyan coins and notes, and pretend buying and selling.

manas.q: Which everyday trip is good for practising money skills?

children.note: Days of the week, morning and evening, and simple daily routines.
Language of the home matters in the early grades.
Children understand new ideas faster when they first hear them in a familiar language.
Grandparents' stories, riddles and songs are rich learning in the indigenous language.
This depends on the school and community. Check with your school.
Art, music and play are real learning, not extras.
Drawing, painting, and making things with clay, paper or waste materials.
Songs, rhymes and traditional dances build memory, rhythm and teamwork.
Running, jumping, skipping and ball games build strong, healthy bodies.
Earlier designs had a separate hygiene and nutrition area; today such topics appear within other areas.

manas.q: Is Hygiene and Nutrition still listed as a separate Grade 1–3 area?

children.note: Families choose one religious education option, depending on what the school offers.
KICD lists CRE, IRE and HRE for Grades 1–3.

manas.q: Which three religious education options are listed for Grades 1–3?

children.note: Ask the school which options it offers and tell them your family's choice.
All options teach respect, honesty, kindness and caring for others.
Much learning happens away from the desk.
Making a chart of the weather, growing beans in a tin, or building a model home.
Planting and watering seeds teaches science, care and patience.
Looking at trees, insects, soil and water sources near the school.
Working in pairs and groups helps children share, listen and solve problems together.
Bottle tops, stones and leaves make cheap counting and art materials.
CBC builds skills and values, not just facts.
The framework names seven, including communication and collaboration, critical thinking and problem solving, and creativity and imagination.

manas.q: How many core competencies does CBC name?

children.note: Telling news, asking questions and listening to others in class.
Trying again after a mistake, and asking 'why?' and 'how?'.
Where available, simple safe use of devices with adult guidance. Check with your school.
Taking turns, caring for books, and greeting others politely.

manas.q: Name two CBC values young children practise daily.

children.note: Telling the truth and helping a classmate who is hurt or sad.
Teachers watch, listen and check work through the year.
Teachers check learning day by day through observation, questions, oral reading and short tasks.

manas.q: What is day-to-day checking of learning by the teacher called?

children.note: Teachers see whether a child can actually do a skill, like reading aloud or counting money.
Samples of a child's work may be kept to show progress over time. Ask your school how it does this.
Schools share progress with parents. Ask the teacher how and when.
KICD's 2019 timeline shows a national assessment at the end of Grade 3. Check the current name and timing with your school or KNEC.

manas.q: At the end of which grade does KICD's timeline show the first national assessment?

children.note: Assessment in these years aims to find where a child needs help, so worry less and support more.
Parents are partners in CBC learning.
Often a small activity: collect leaves, count items at home, or ask a grandparent a question.

children.topic: Help, don't do it for them
children.note: Guide and encourage, but let the child do the work and make mistakes.
Use old boxes, bottle tops, seeds and newspaper for projects. Ask the teacher if unsure what is needed.
Visit or message the teacher about how your child is doing and how to help.
Count steps, plates or chapatis together; a market trip is a maths lesson.
Regular sleep, a good breakfast and a quiet homework corner help children learn.
Ten minutes of reading together each day makes a big difference.
Read stories to your child, then let them read to you.
Read in English, Kiswahili and your home language.
Ask: what happened? How did they feel? What would you do?
Signs, labels, newspapers and matatu stickers are reading practice too.
Family stories, riddles and songs grow vocabulary just as well.
Community and school libraries lend books for free or at low cost. Check what is near you.
After Grade 3, children move to upper primary.
Upper primary is Grade 4 to Grade 6, part of Middle School.

manas.q: Which grades come after lower primary?

children.note: Activity-based areas grow into subjects such as Science and Technology, Social Studies and Agriculture.

manas.q: Name a new learning area that appears in Grade 4.

children.note: Children are expected to read and write more independently.
Keep the reading habit, practise times tables and build curiosity.
